blocks.x: This summer’s FIFA World Cup yielded some of the most cutthroat competition the sports world has ever seen. I’m speaking, of course, about the global battle for bag supremacy. Star footballers Jude Bellingham, Kylian Mbappé, and Virgil van Dijk stepped off planes with luxury bags costing more than most mortgage payments. Spanish wunderkind Lamine Yamal strolled through stadiums carrying an all-star lineup, including a Dior Archie and an enormous tweed Chanel shopping tote. But it was Erling Haaland, Norway’s Viking-like striker, who stole the golden man bag (and blew up social feeds) for his rotation of rare Hermès HACs, the French house’s elongated predecessor to the almighty Birkin. Together, these men pushed the Age of Bag Enlightenment to new heights.

To put it another way: Guys are into bags. Luxe bags. Sumptuous bags. Rare unicorn bags. For a subset of fashion-aware men, they are the equivalent of collecting watches or vintage Porsche 911s: a hobby, a reason to nerd out, a statement, and a flex all in one. For a few years now, famous faces like Jacob Elordi, Harry Styles, and A$AP Rocky have made opulent handbags a staple of their carrying-a-coffee-in-SoHo ensembles. And, according to the data, a legion of not-so-famous fellas are following suit. Depop—now indisputably the eBay for Gen Z—reports that men’s bag purchases are up 116 percent year over year. Searches on the platform for men’s bags from Bottega Veneta and Hermès, in particular, tripled over the summer.

Scroll down and you can understand why. Every legendary luxury brand, from Marni to Fendi to Loewe, is flooding the zone with duffels and crossbodies and carryalls aimed squarely at men who’ve realized that their everyday bag can say more than “I’m running late for an 8:30 a.m. touch-base.”

Michael Fisher, a stylist for celebrities like Dan Levy and Sebastian Stan, calls the big-bag blowup a modernization of an age-old status symbol. “I think guys see it as, I’m successful, I need a good bag,” he says. “Kind of like what the briefcase was to your father.”

Vik Soni, a 42-year-old New York City radiation oncologist, splashed out on a Saint Laurent hobo because he wanted something plush but presentable that could keep up with work, gym, and dinners out. “I care about fashion,” he says. “If I have a backpack, that might be one hundred percent functional but zero percent complementary to whatever setting I’m in.”

Which isn’t to say that every man has joined Saint Laurent–carrying Soni in appreciating the beauty of a luxe bag. “If you want to splurge every now and then, is it going to be on a handbag if you’re a straight guy?” wonders Ethan Sawyer, a 35-year-old journalist getting around Vancouver with his trusty L.L.Bean tote. “It feels a bit trendy, while something like a watch feels more timeless. I struggle to picture a reality in two or three years where I’m really happy that I spent $7,000 on what is essentially a purse.”

Sawyer’s watch analogy makes more sense than he may know. Before becoming the bag whisperer known to his more than 60,000 TikTok followers as @jasoninparis, Jason (he declined to provide a last name) was a serious watch fiend. Then, last year, he bought his “gateway bag”: a Louis Vuitton Speedy P9, part of Pharrell’s debut collection for the maison. That’s led to an ever-growing collection of about 30 luxury bags, like an impossible-to-get Hermès Kelly Pochette or a sold-out Schiaparelli Bijoux Secret.

Wearing dialed-in fits, he’ll show off the latest white whale he’s landed—like when he mentions a rare crystal-and-pearl-encrusted Louis Vuitton Keepall Bandoulière 45 from the spring-summer 2026 runway show—of which Jason explains, “There’s only three left in the world....” At which point he pauses for effect, before continuing: “And that’s because I got one.” Cue the reveal, the bag glittering for his phone camera.

“I don’t buy bags as an investment, I buy bags to wear,” Jason tells me. He approaches them with the same detail-loving geekery he brought to collecting watches. “The way I appreciate mechanical movements, I care about saddle stitching. I kind of obsess about leather.”
But there is a difference between watch guys and bag guys, in Jason’s view. “I think men wear watches to impress men,” he says. “But I think bags can impress secure men.”
